problem: The biasing direction is mixed up. ANDing a stage output with a control bit pushes the probability of a 1 below 0.5 (more 0s), which is what a wide OR gate needs; ORing pushes it above 0.5 (more 1s), which is what a wide AND gate needs. As written, the AND weighting is paired with 'wide AND gates need many 1s', which is the opposite of what that hardware does.
fix: A weighted LFSR gates each stage output with a control bit. ANDing the output with the control pushes the probability of a 1 below 0.5, so the stream carries many 0s — good for wide OR gates, which need all-zero inputs. ORing the output with the control pushes the probability of a 1 above 0.5 — good for wide AND gates, which need all-one inputs.

problem: 'each scan chain is broken open and its flip-flops are stitched into the LFSR, so a vector is shifted in over several clocks' describes the wrong mechanism. In test-per-scan the TPG drives the scan-in pin and the scan-out pin feeds the ORA; the chain is not merged into the LFSR, and the shift-in time follows from the chain length, not from stitching.
fix: In test-per-scan the TPG drives the scan-in input of each chain, L shift clocks push one vector into the chain, one capture clock loads the response, and the shifted-out bits go to the ORA. A vector therefore costs L + 1 clocks.

problem: The symbol L stands for two different quantities: length of the longest scan chain in Section 1 and LFSR period in Section 2. A student flipping between the two formulas can carry the wrong meaning across.
fix: Keep L for scan chain length in T = N × (L + 1) and use P (or L_period) for the LFSR period, writing P = 2ⁿ − 1.

problem: The clause 'so only one XOR delay per clock' has no verb and reads as a fragment; the comparison with the external-XOR form is left implicit.
fix: In internal-XOR form the XOR gates sit between stages, so the feedback passes through only one XOR per clock and the register can run faster; the trade-off is a less obvious tap table.
